title: Cabernet Sauvignon
description: The world's most planted red grape: blackcurrant, cedar and structure, from the Médoc to Napa.
L: Describe Cabernet Sauvignon's flavours and structure

Cabernet Sauvignon gives deep-coloured wines with blackcurrant, black cherry, cedar, mint and sometimes green pepper. It has high tannin and high acidity, so it ages well. It is the world's most planted wine grape, about 340,000 hectares, grown in almost every wine country.

In 1996, DNA research at UC Davis showed that Cabernet Sauvignon is a natural cross of Cabernet Franc and Sauvignon Blanc, probably in 17th century Bordeaux. Its small, thick-skinned berries, with a high ratio of skin and seed to juice, explain its colour and tannin. It also resists rot and frost well, since it buds late.
Which two grapes are the parents of Cabernet Sauvignon?
DNA testing in 1996 showed it was a cross of Cabernet Franc and Sauvignon Blanc.

Look for deep colour, a nose of blackcurrant with cedar, mint or pencil shavings, and a palate with firm tannin and fresh acidity. In cooler sites, a green pepper or leafy note. In warmer ones, ripe black fruit and sometimes eucalyptus. It often sits in oak, adding vanilla and toast.
Cabernet Sauvignon buds late, which helps it avoid spring frost.
Yes. Late budding protects it from frost, but late ripening means it needs a warm site.
Cabernet Sauvignon gives blackcurrant, cedar and firm tannin
It's a 17th century cross of Cabernet Franc and Sauvignon Blanc
Small, thick-skinned berries give colour, tannin and ageing power
Explain how it adapts to different places

Cabernet's classic home is Bordeaux's Left Bank. It's the leading red in Napa Valley, Chile's Maipo, Australia's Coonawarra and Margaret River, Washington State and South Africa's Stellenbosch. In Italy it's key to Bolgheri's Super Tuscans. It also grows in Argentina, China and Spain.

As a late ripener, Cabernet needs a long, warm season. In cool places it can taste green, from pyrazines that only break down when fully ripe. Warm, dry sites with well-drained soils suit it best. That's why it does so well on gravel and in sunny, irrigated New World regions.
Match each region to its Cabernet character.
Place changes Cabernet's accent while its core stays.

Cabernet's thick skins resist rot, its late budding avoids frost, and it keeps its character in many soils and climates. Growers find it reliable, and consumers recognise the name. That's how it became the world's most planted wine grape, overtaking others in the 1990s.
Why can Cabernet taste green in cool climates?
Pyrazines that only break down with full ripeness
Pyrazines give green pepper notes; full ripeness reduces them.
Cabernet grows in almost every wine country
It needs warmth and drainage to ripen fully
Its resistance and recognisability made it the most planted grape
Explain why Cabernet suits the Médoc
Name the key Left Bank appellations

The Médoc and Graves, on the left bank of the Gironde and Garonne, have deep gravel soils left by ancient rivers. Gravel drains well and stores the sun's heat, releasing it at night. That helps Cabernet ripen in Bordeaux's moderate, maritime climate. The best châteaux sit on gravel mounds close to the estuary.

Left Bank reds are usually led by Cabernet Sauvignon, often 60 to 80%, with Merlot to add flesh, and smaller amounts of Cabernet Franc and Petit Verdot. Blending also spreads risk: in a cool year, Merlot ripens when Cabernet struggles. The result is structured, cedar-scented wine that can age for decades.
Why is Merlot blended with Cabernet on the Left Bank?
To add flesh and reduce risk in cool years
Merlot fills Cabernet's mid-palate and ripens earlier, which helps in cool vintages.

Pauillac, home to three of the five First Growths, makes powerful, cedar-scented wines. Margaux is more perfumed and elegant. Saint-Julien sits between them. Saint-Estèphe, further north, is firmer, with more clay. Pessac-Léognan, in the Graves, makes both reds and whites, including Haut-Brion.
Match each appellation to its style.
Small differences in soil and position shape each style.
Gravel helps Cabernet ripen in the Médoc
Left Bank blends are Cabernet-led, with Merlot
Pauillac, Margaux, Saint-Julien and Saint-Estèphe are key

Methoxypyrazines are aromatic compounds that smell of green pepper, cut grass and leaves. Humans can detect them at a few parts per trillion. They are found in the Cabernet family: Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Carmenère, Merlot and Sauvignon Blanc. In small amounts they add freshness; in excess, they taste unripe.
Green pepper at parts per trillion

Pyrazines form early in the berry and break down as it ripens, especially with sunlight on the bunches. Cool, cloudy seasons and shaded fruit keep them high. Warm, sunny sites reduce them. This is why a Cabernet from a cool year in Bordeaux may show green notes, while one from Napa rarely does.
Pyrazine levels in grapes rise steadily as they ripen.
Not true. Pyrazines are highest before veraison and fall as grapes ripen, especially in sunlight.

Growers reduce pyrazines by removing leaves around bunches early in the season, letting sunlight reach the fruit. They control vigour so the canopy isn't too dense. They pick later for riper flavour, but must watch sugar and alcohol rising. In the winery, careful sorting removes green material.
Which help lower pyrazine levels in Cabernet?
Pyrazines smell of green pepper and grass
They fall as grapes ripen, especially in sunlight
Leaf removal and balanced canopies help manage them

Napa Valley has a warm, dry Mediterranean climate, with fog cooling mornings. Cabernet Sauvignon is the leading grape and commands some of the world's highest grape prices. The style is ripe and powerful, with blackcurrant, cassis, chocolate and often new French oak, and alcohol of 14.5% or more.

In 1976, British merchant Steven Spurrier organised a blind tasting in Paris. French judges ranked a 1973 Stag's Leap Wine Cellars Cabernet ahead of top Bordeaux, including Mouton Rothschild and Haut-Brion. The result made headlines and showed the world that California could rival France.
Which wine won the red section of the 1976 Judgment of Paris?
Stag's Leap Wine Cellars Cabernet Sauvignon
The 1973 Stag's Leap Cabernet topped the red wines, ahead of famous Bordeaux.

Chile's Maipo makes ripe Cabernet with a minty, herbal note, often good value. Coonawarra, in Australia, on terra rossa soil, gives elegant wines with mint and eucalyptus. Margaret River has a Bordeaux-like, maritime style. Washington State gives ripe fruit with fresh acidity. Stellenbosch blends power with freshness.
Match each region to its Cabernet note.
Each New World region has its own Cabernet accent.
Napa makes ripe, powerful, expensive Cabernet
The 1976 Judgment of Paris put California on the map
Maipo, Coonawarra, Margaret River and Washington add their own styles

Cabernet's firm tannin and dark fruit call for red meat: steak, roast beef, lamb. Fat and protein soften the tannin. Peppercorn sauce and mushrooms go well. Hard aged cheeses like Comté or aged Cheddar work too. Avoid delicate fish and very spicy food, which make it taste harsh.

Serve at 16 to 18 degrees. Decant young, structured Cabernets for an hour or two. Top Bordeaux and Napa can age 20 to 40 years, gaining cedar, tobacco, leather and earth while tannins soften. Everyday Cabernets are best within three to five years.
Why does Cabernet Sauvignon go so well with steak?
Fat and protein soften its tannin
Tannin binds to protein and fat, so each softens the other.
Old Bordeaux and Napa throw sediment. Stand the bottle upright for a day before opening, then decant slowly in front of a light.
Which aromas develop in Cabernet as it ages?
Green apple is a young white wine aroma.
Cabernet suits steak, lamb and aged cheese
Serve at 16 to 18 degrees and decant young wines
Which grapes are Cabernet Sauvignon's parents?
Match each place to its role in Cabernet's story.
Sunlight on the bunches helps lower pyrazine levels.
Yes. Pyrazines break down as grapes ripen, especially when exposed to light.
Left Bank Bordeaux soils are mainly ____.
Gravel drains and stores heat, helping Cabernet ripen.
Cabernet gives blackcurrant, cedar, firm tannin and acidity
Bordeaux's Left Bank is its model; Napa its New World star
Pyrazines give green notes when it's not fully ripe
It suits red meat and can age for decades
